The problem is that it's trying to read form data (multipart), and for that it requires the package `python-multipart` installed.

It is documented in the docs in FastAPI and Starlette, but forgetting to install it and running the app ends up in that behavior that is not explicit nor obvious. Everything works normally, except that specific *path operation*, that only breaks after a receiving a request (which is worse).

To make things more complex, the package required is `python-multipart`. But there's another Python package called just `multipart`.

And both packages are imported as:

```Python
import multipart
```

This can lead to a problem that is really difficult to debug: an environment with both packages installed, in some runs could import the correct package and everything would work, but in other runs, it could import the other package, which would cause problems. That would make it one of those scary ghost bugs that disappear and appear. :bug: :ghost: 

 And even worse, the problems will only show up *after* receiving a request in a path operation that requires reading form data, not at start up.

### The solution you would like

<!-- Replace this with your own content -->

In FastAPI, the main ways to get form data are quite explicit, using `Form`, `UploadFile`, `bytes`.

That means that it's possible to detect that a path operation will try to read form data on initialization.

I would like FastAPI to raise an error and crash fast when there's a *path operation* that uses something that requires to read form data, right on initialization (while creating the instances).

In Starlette (or in FastAPI when using the request directly), there's no way to know if the code will try to access form data from the request.

But in FastAPI, as it is declared in function parameters that are read during initialization, it would be possible to error out early.

It should log an error saying that form data requires `python-multipart` and then raise the exception. This would be triggered right while starting an application.

But it would only raise an exception if there's a path operation that actually requires form data, otherwise, everything would work as normal.

It should ideally also detect if the imported `multipart` is the correct one or not. If the incorrect one is installed/imported, it should log an error informing that clearly, explaining that `multipart` is not compatible with `python-multipart`, that the user has to uninstall `multipart` and then install `python-multipart`.

There's a point in code that decides if a *path operation* should read from JSON or from Form data while creating the request body field for a *path operation*. Whatever does the check about `python-multipart`, would ideally run from that same point.

Title: BackgroundTasks won't run: AttributeError: 'function' object has no attribute 'tasks'

### One-line Fix

In your `/orders` view function, use `background_tasks: BackgroundTasks` instead of `background_tasks=BackgroundTasks`

```python
@app.post("/orders")
async def create(request: Request, background_tasks: BackgroundTasks):
	...
```

---

### Why your code didn't work

[`BackgroundTasks`](https://github.com/encode/starlette/blob/20d24a86b877e21ed002abb1668e69002850f38b/starlette/background.py#L31-L43) is a class that should be instantiated before use, so `background_tasks=BackgroundTasks` won't do quite what you expect it to.

FastAPI uses [Dependency Injection](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/dependencies/) to provide you with an _instance_ of `BackgroundTasks` ([source](https://github.com/tiangolo/fastapi/blob/26f725d259c5dbe3654f221e608b14412c6b40da/fastapi/dependencies/utils.py#L566-L569)) that's [automatically queued](https://github.com/encode/starlette/blob/20d24a86b877e21ed002abb1668e69002850f38b/starlette/responses.py#L160-L163) by Starlette after your view function returns a response.

(I'd encourage you to read through the linked source code to firm up your understanding of the problem)

If you look at Starlette's implementation of `add_task` you'll see something like:

```python
class BackgroundTasks(...):
	...
    def add_task(self, func, *args, **kwargs):
        task = BackgroundTask(func, *args, **kwargs)
        self.tasks.append(task)
```

Where `self` is meant to be the instance of `BackgroundTasks` injected by FastAPI.

In your current code (where `background_tasks=BackgroundTasks`) when you call `background_tasks.add_task(order_completed, order)` you're effectively doing:

```python
BackgroundTasks.add_task(order_completed, order)
# Which effectively does:
order_completed.tasks.append(BackgroundTask(order))
```

In the 'fixed' code (where `background_tasks` is an _instance_ of `BackgroundTasks`) when you do `background_tasks.add_task(order_completed, order)` you'd effectively be doing:

```python
BackgroundTasks.add_task(background_tasks, order_completed, order)
# Which effectively does:
background_tasks.tasks.append(BackgroundTask(order_completed, order))
```

See the FastAPI docs on [Background Tasks](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/background-tasks/) for more info.

Title: Deprecating BaseHTTPMiddleware

> This is a rather bold move to make given the usage of BaseHTTPMiddleware in the wild, so let’s pause and think it through.

I agree. I realize this is pretty aggressive proposal and recognize that it's a long shot for it to be accepted, but I hope that it can at least lead to some good discussion.

> I’m sure there’s been discussion before (are there any links available?), but jotting down some thoughts and questions…

There are lots of general issues related to BaseHTTPMiddleware, the last/clearest I can think of is https://github.com/encode/starlette/pull/1640#discussion_r880925576.

> In general, what’s the migration path going to be like for users of BaseHTTPMiddleware? 
Should we start by exploring how FastAPI could do without? It’s still relying on `@app.middleware` extensively. If the hundreds of thousands (maybe?) of FastAPI users get this deprecation warning, what action should they take to keep their systems running? Certainly the action might be on some intermediate dependency maintenance team. Does this mean we should first help folks migrate, _then_ deprecate?

I think there are several ways to tackle this:
- Better documentation on writing pure ASGI middleware (#1656 
- Contributing downstream to prominent libraries using BaseHTTPMiddleware (https://github.com/trallnag/prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator/pull/139, https://github.com/python-discord/forms-backend/pull/173, will need more)
- Responding to the inevitable inflow of issues along the lines of "how do I convert this middleware to pure ASGI"
- _Maybe_ providing some sort of simple middleware that does not suffer from the pitfalls of BaseHTTPMiddleware. I've been playing around with an idea [here](https://github.com/encode/starlette/compare/master...adriangb:safe-basehttpmiddleware?expand=1), but maybe other options like a "hook" style API for pure ASGI middleware.

> What does addressing the two problems mentioned in the docs (context vars, background tasks) look like with pure ASGI middleware?

Basically: nothing. These problems simple don't exist with pure ASGI middleware.

> What do existing examples in the BaseHTTPMiddleware docs look like using pure ASGI middleware?

+1 on this. I think we should replace any examples not specific to BaseHTTPMiddleware with pure ASGI middleware, independently of the outcome of this proposal.

> While I reckon the limitations of BaseHTTPMiddleware, and the fact that currently users expect certain things to work that don’t, I also fear « pure ASGI middleware all the things » might be really off putting a lot of folks who’d like to do very simple edits to requests or responses.

I've found that often a pure ASGI middleware isn't necessarily more LOC or that ugly _once you know how to write it_ (I admit there is a learning curve). Things that are ugly with pure ASGI middleware (like intercepting the request or response body byte stream) tend to be impossible or buggy with BaseHTTPMiddleware. Pure ASGI also has the _huge_ ecosystem benefit of not being coupled to Starlette. So maybe pure ASGI all the things isn't _that_ bad.

```python
class async_stream:

    def __init__(self, request):
        """Use internal checker to skip behaviour."""

        self.req = request
        self.phase = 0
        self.chk = False

        return self

    async def __anext__(self):
        """ Return the next stream.
        Use StopAsyncIteration to cancel iterator.
        Equivalent to "return" in a generator function.
        """

        if self.phase == 0:
            if not self.chk:
                if hasattr(self.req, "_body"):
                    self.chk = True
                    return self._body
            else:
                self.step += 1
                self.chk = True
                raise StopAsyncIteration

        elif self.phase == 1:
            if self.req._stream_consumed:
                raise RuntimeError("Stream consumed")
            self.req._stream_consumed = True
            self.phase += 1

        elif self.phase == 2:
            if not self.chk:
                message = await self.req._receive()
                if message["type"] == "http.request":
                    body = message.get("body", b"")
                    if body:
                        return body
                    if not message.get("more_body", False):
                        self.chk = True
                elif message["type"] == "http.disconnect":
                    raise ClientDisconnect()
            else:
                self.phase += 1

        elif self.phase == 3:
            return b""
        else:
            raise StopAsyncIteration
```

I build [a library](https://github.com/yaal-coop/pydantic-scim2) where I provide a bunch of pydantic Models which have a common behavior. Among the common behaviors shared between all the models is how to discriminate them.

As I find the `Discriminator` + `Tag` declaration a bit tedious, I provide a `tagged_union` method that does the job, so users of the library do not have to think about discriminators: they just provide models.

Here is how it looks like (though it is simplified, as the discriminator in my use case is not a litteral):

```python
from typing import Annotated
from typing import Generic
from typing import List
from typing import Literal
from typing import TypeVar
from typing import Union
from typing import get_args
from typing import get_origin

from pydantic import BaseModel
from pydantic import Discriminator
from pydantic import Tag


def tagged_union(*types):
    types = Union[types]
    types = get_args(types) if get_origin(types) == Union else [types]

    def get_discriminator_value(payload):
        return payload["discriminator"]

    def get_tag(type):
        discriminator, *_ = get_args(type.model_fields["discriminator"].annotation)
        return Tag(discriminator)

    tagged_resources = [Annotated[type, get_tag(type)] for type in types]
    return Annotated[
        Union[tuple(tagged_resources)], Discriminator(get_discriminator_value)
    ]


T = TypeVar("T")


class Foo(BaseModel):
    discriminator: Literal["foo"]


class Bar(BaseModel):
    discriminator: Literal["bar"]


class Model(BaseModel, Generic[T]):
```

- **Python Version**: 3.12
- **OS**: Linux (WSL2)

When the same discriminated union is referenced through multiple nested model paths, `model_rebuild()` incorrectly raises `TypeError: Value 'X' for discriminator 'Y' mapped to multiple choices`, even though:
- Each discriminator field name is unique across different unions
- Each discriminator value is unique within its union

```python
from __future__ import annotations
from typing import Union, Optional, Literal, TYPE_CHECKING
from typing_extensions import Annotated
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

# Define a discriminated union
class StatReference(BaseModel):
    attribute_reference_type: Literal["stat_reference"] = "stat_reference"
    base: str

class ResourceReference(BaseModel):
    attribute_reference_type: Literal["resource_reference"] = "resource_reference"
    base: str

AttributeReference = Annotated[
    Union[StatReference, ResourceReference],
    Field(discriminator="attribute_reference_type")
]

# Use this union in multiple nested paths
class ResourceCheck(BaseModel):
    attribute: AttributeReference  # Path 1

class ResourceCondition(BaseModel):
    condition_type: Literal["resource_condition"] = "resource_condition"
    check: ResourceCheck

class StatusCondition(BaseModel):
    condition_type: Literal["status_condition"] = "status_condition"
    has_status: str

    Union[StatusCondition, ResourceCondition],
    Field(discriminator="condition_type")
]

class ModifierValue(BaseModel):
    attribute: AttributeReference  # Path 2

class Modifier(BaseModel):
    condition: Condition  # Contains ResourceCondition -> ResourceCheck -> AttributeReference
    modifier: ModifierValue  # Also contains AttributeReference

# Rebuild triggers the error
Modifier.model_rebuild()
```

```
TypeError: Value 'stat_reference' for discriminator 'attribute_reference_type' mapped to multiple choices
```

`model_rebuild()` should succeed because:
1. Within the `AttributeReference` union, `"stat_reference"` uniquely maps to `StatReference`
2. The discriminator field `attribute_reference_type` is unique (no other union uses this field name)
3. The union is simply being reused in multiple locations (standard compositional design)

`model_rebuild()` traverses the model tree and encounters `AttributeReference` through multiple paths:
- `Modifier` -> `condition` -> `ResourceCondition` -> `check` -> `attribute` -> `AttributeReference`

1. **Namespaced discriminator values**: Changed from `"stat"` to `"stat_reference"` to ensure absolutely no possible collision - still fails
2. **`from __future__ import annotations`**: Applied to avoid explicit forward reference strings - still requires rebuild

- These unions are composed into larger structures

### Description

When using an `alias_generator` and a `validation alias`, the `alias_generator` does not override the serialization alias (which is **not** set)[^1].
This is very unintuitive, since if a normal alias is set, it overrides default value for serialization alias as well[^2]. 
Setting `alias_priority=1` on every field fixes this, but it also removes the `validation alias`[^3].

My suggestion would be making making `alias_generator` override both unset `validation_alias` and unset `serialization_alias`. Additionally there should be a `default_alias_priority` field added to the `model_config`, so that even when adding a `serialization_alias`, a common style can be guaranteed.

**Why is this needed?**
In our FastApi project, we want to return a JSON object, with CamelCase. In python we want to use snake case though. We get some data from another api, so I added a `validation_alias` to Model. This however broke our API, since the resulting JSON was not in CamelCase anymore.

[^2]: See `foo_bar2`.
[^3]: See `foo_bar3`.
[^4]: See https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/concepts/alias/#alias-priority
